Hi Max,

Renjin supports a sort of basic dependency injection for methods, see:
http://www.renjin.org/documentation/contributor-guide.html#contextual-arguments

You can get access to the current Session object by declaring your method this way:

public void myFunction(@Current Session session, String firstArgument, SEXP secondArgument) {
   //...
}

HTH,
Alex

Hi Anton,
R can be tricky to wrap your head around when first coming from a different language. It helps a lot to think of R as "a lisp" - there's a bit of extra syntax thrown into make it look a bit more like fortran, but in the end it's all parens!

Have you seen the page on "moving data between R and Java" ?
http://docs.renjin.org/en/latest/moving-data-between-java-and-r-code.html#pulling-data-from-r-into-java

You might also look at the general documentation for the javax.script API:
http://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/scripting/programmer_guide/

If your "Person" bean has the normal getters and setters, then you should be able to pass the List<Person> into Renjin and then, you can certainly use familiar java idioms such as:

sum <- 0
for(p in persons) {
    sum <- sum + p$age
}
avg <- sum / length(persons)

But then of course you will miss out on the power of R as an array language. You can turn your list into an "atomic vector" by using idioms from R's functional side:

age <- sapply(persons, function(p) { return p$age })

If you do print(age), then you'll see something like this:

> print(age)
[1] 14 3 25 52  1

You could do the same for other properties of your bean

> name <- sapply(persons, function(p) p$name)
> print(name)
[1] "Bob"  "Karl" "Sam"

Then you can use R's more fluent functions:

> mean(age)

And so on...

HTH

Alex

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anton,

Maybe you could take a look at SciCom.  SciCom is a Ruby wrapper for Renjing, but since SciCom targets JRuby (JVM), at the end it is all Java, and thus can be packed in a jar and served through a web server.

When I started SciCom, my first idea was to actually interface with Renjin SEXP, but then I realized that much of R power could be lost if I tried that, as R is very dynamic and can deal with heterogeneous inputs. For instance, arrays of different dimensions that get dynamically expanded according to some R rules.  At the end, SciCom "just" translates Ruby syntax to R strings (that the user never sees) and calls eval.  For the user, it seems that she is coding in Ruby, on the background, it is all just R code.

If you have questions, feel free to contact me.

Cheers,

Rodrigo

messages.subject_clean: Is there any reason that Renjin remove the namespace related functions from R base?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Max,
Namespaces are one of the few areas where we're not using a GNU R component even though it's implemented in the R language.

The reason for this is that  namespace.R is heavily coupled to the file system and to the layout used by GNU R specifically.

This made it difficult to support use cases like loading packages from the classpath so that R packages built for renjin could be distributed and managed using the same tools and ecosystem that benefit java developer.

I made some attempt to adapt the code to these ends, but ultimately it was more straightforward to pull packaging up into the interpreter itself.

The bulk of the logic now sits in NamespaceRegistry, but the actual mechanism of accessing package resource metadata is done via the extension point PackageLoader interface.

We currently have two implementations: ClasspathPackageLoader, and AetherPackageLoader, which loads packages via maven/ivy repositories.

Is there something not working or differently than expected?

Alex

messages.body_plain:
Anton,

I´m no specialist in R/Renjin, so read with care!

When you read a csv file in R, my understanding is that every column of the csv becomes a vector and all those vectors are collected into an R dataframe.  Let´s call this dataframe 'df'.  Now if you want to access the second column from df, you can do df[[2]] (if you do df[2] then this is again a list and not the individual object... kind of weird, but this is R!).  This should be something like a Java::OrgRenjinSexp::DoubleArrayVector (IntArrayVector), etc. which is actually a Java object.  You can then call method toDoubleArrayUnsafe() or toDoubleArray() to either have access, respectively, to the vector or to a copy of the vector.

Your Java developers will have to work with all those vectors, or you can copy every vector and build an array out of them (not efficient, but could be good enough).

You could probably also work the other way around, i.e., read the csv file onto a java array and then pass this java array to Renjin as a Renjin matrix.  In Renjin you can convert the matrix to a dataframe (and then add column and row names to the dataframe).  At this point you can run any R script on this dataframe.  One important thing to remember is that R organizes matrix and arrays in column-major order and java arrays are organized in row-major order (I think).

Actually there seems to be a bug in the read.csv method and not actually in converting strings to dates.  I was able to read the csv file that you sent in another post.  However, I had to read it with

data = read.csv("org.csv", header = false, sep = ";").

Dear Renjin community,

I am working with time series data in Renjin. I currently met this problem: (all codes in R)

Given 2 characters of date, for example:
t1 <- "Tue Feb 17 10:30:00 2015"
t2 <- "Tue Feb 17 16:20:24 2015"

And change the data type to date:
tt1 <- strptime(t1, "%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y")
tt2 <- strptime(t2, "%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y")

Calculate the time difference:
td <- tt2 - tt1

If in GNU R, the result is "Time difference of 5.84 hours"

But in Renjin, the result is "Time difference of -10 mins"

messages.body_plain:
Hi Max,

If you're on a *nix system, you can run "lsof -p <pid>" when renjin is running to see if the JVM has loaded the native libraries.

You can also turn on logging for "org.netlib.*" to see which versions gets loaded, or check LAPACK.getInstance().getClass().getName() to see which is in use.

Best,
Alex
